rationale: B wins because it keeps its hands on the facts instead of decorating around them. A's strongest reach, "Mindbody Owns the Studio Software, the Consumer Marketplace, and Now the AI That Fills Both," is a smart business question but the headline sells a ClassPass connection the update does not prove. B's "A 22% drop in no-shows: what Mindbody's AI pilot proves and what it doesn't" is less flashy and more usable: it knows the first reporter reply will be methodology, not applause.
gaps_in_A: "Rolling Out to 50,000 Studios" overclaims reach. The update says Mindbody powers booking for over 50,000 studios and salons, not that this assistant is rolling out to all of them.
"Now the AI That Fills Both" leans too hard on ClassPass. The set later asks whether the systems are separate, but the headline has already spent a fact it does not have.
"While Fitness Apps Race to Build AI Coaches" imports a market narrative the update did not supply. It may be true, but it needs named contrast cases before it can carry a contrarian angle.

The refusal of "Bundled pricing / AI monetization angle" is too quick. Bundled pricing is one of the few hard business facts in the update and can support a vertical-SaaS monetization story if the company will explain it.
gaps_in_B: "What an empty spot costs a boutique studio" is useful but conditional. Without the "one named studio" it asks for, it is not a pitch yet; it is a shopping list.
"Why Mindbody isn't charging extra for AI" is real but thin. The retention and owner-expectation frame needs an executive or competitive proof, or it becomes a neat inference in a better pitch.
"salon trade outlet" drifts from the launch. The assistant is for boutique fitness and wellness studios; do not send a class-cancellation story to the wrong vertical.
B correctly kills "ClassPass users will now fill your studio's empty spots," but it underuses the safer ClassPass question: platform strategy without claiming integration.
